## Overview

LTBI diagnostic tests—such as interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA: QuantiFERON, T-SPOT.TB) and the tuberculin skin test (TST)—have imperfect sensitivity and specificity. Furthermore, clinical cohorts differ in how diagnostic test results and active TB progression follow-up are structured:

1. **Population-Level vs. Individual-Level Latent-Class Coupling (`coupling`):** Whether we only link population-level prevalence $\pi$ across modules, or jointly marginalize over each individual's latent infection status $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ across their baseline test result(s) $\mathbf{x}_i$ and progression outcome $(t_i, d_i)$.
2. **Single vs. Multiple Diagnostic Tests ($K \ge 1$):** Combining $K = 2$ tests (e.g., IGRA + TST) on the same individuals provides conditional latent-class information about sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence.
3. **All-Comers vs. Test-Positive Follow-Up (`cohort_type`):** When only test-positive individuals ($X_{i,1} = 1$) are followed for progression, false positives cannot progress to active TB, so the uncured fraction is the **Positive Predictive Value ($\text{PPV}$)** rather than the population prevalence $\pi$.
4. **Covariates & Parametric Survival Families (`covariates`, `surv_dist`):** Adjusting prevalence by baseline risk factors and comparing Gompertz, Weibull, and Exponential progression hazards.

---

## Mathematical Formulation

### 1. Imperfect Diagnostic Tests ($K \ge 1$) and Covariates

Let $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denote true baseline LTBI status for individual $i$, with covariate-adjusted prevalence:

$$
P(Z_i = 1) = \pi_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i), \qquad \eta_i = \alpha + \mathbf{x}_{\text{cov}, i}^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

Suppose individual $i$ undergoes $K \ge 1$ diagnostic tests $\mathbf{X}_i = (X_{i,1}, \dots, X_{i,K})$ with sensitivities $\text{sens}_k = P(X_{i,k} = 1 \mid Z_i = 1)$ and specificities $\text{spec}_k = P(X_{i,k} = 0 \mid Z_i = 0)$. Conditional on $Z_i$, the test likelihood is:

$$
P(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 1) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \text{sens}_k^{x_{i,k}} (1 - \text{sens}_k)^{1 - x_{i,k}}, \qquad
P(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 0) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} (1 - \text{spec}_k)^{x_{i,k}} \text{spec}_k^{1 - x_{i,k}}.
$$

Marginalizing over $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ gives the marginal test likelihood for individual $i$:

$$
P(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}_i) = (1 - \pi_i) P(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 0) + \pi_i P(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 1).
$$

---

### 2. Population Coupling vs. Individual Latent-Class Coupling

When a linked cohort observes **both** diagnostic test results $\mathbf{x}_i$ and progression follow-up $(t_i, d_i)$ on the same individuals $i = 1, \dots, N_{\text{surv}}$, `EvidSynthTB` supports two coupling mechanisms:

#### A. Population-Level Modular Coupling (`coupling = "population"`)
Treats the diagnostic test results and survival times as two separate modular likelihoods that share the population prevalence parameter $\pi_i$, marginalizing over $Z_i$ independently in each module:

$$
L_i^{\text{pop}}(\mathbf{x}_i, t_i, d_i) =
\Big[ (1 - \pi_{\text{diag}, i}) P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 0) + \pi_{\text{diag}, i} P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 1) \Big]
\times
\Big[ \pi_{\text{surv}, i} f_u(t_i) \Big]^{d_i} \Big[ (1 - \pi_{\text{surv}, i}) + \pi_{\text{surv}, i} S_u(t_i) \Big]^{1 - d_i}.
$$

#### B. Individual-Level Latent-Class Coupling (`coupling = "latent_class"`)
Recognizes that the **same** latent infection state $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ governs both individual $i$'s baseline test results $\mathbf{x}_i$ and their ability to progress to active TB $(t_i, d_i)$. Marginalizing $Z_i$ over the joint outcome $(\mathbf{X}_i, T_i, d_i)$ yields:

$$
L_i^{\text{LC}}(\mathbf{x}_i, t_i, d_i) =
\begin{cases}
\pi_i \, P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 1) \, f_u(t_i) & \text{if } d_i = 1 \text{ (active TB progression confirms } Z_i = 1\text{)}, \\[6pt]
(1 - \pi_i) \, P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 0) + \pi_i \, P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 1) \, S_u(t_i) & \text{if } d_i = 0 \text{ (right-censored at } t_i\text{)}.
\end{cases}
$$

Notice two critical properties of $L_i^{\text{LC}}$:
1. Every individual who progresses to active TB ($d_i = 1$) is known with certainty to have been truly infected ($Z_i = 1$), so their baseline test result directly informs test sensitivity via $P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 1)$.
2. Under the **Cut** model (`model = "cut"`, Stage 2) with `"latent_class"` coupling, Stage 2 conditions each censored person's survival mixture on their individual test-updated posterior infection probability $\text{PPV}(\mathbf{x}_i) = P(Z_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i)$:

$$
\text{PPV}(\mathbf{x}_i) = P(Z_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{\pi_i \, P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 1)}{(1 - \pi_i) \, P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 0) + \pi_i \, P(\mathbf{x}_i \mid Z_i = 1)}.
$$

---

### 3. Test-Positive Subgroup Follow-Up (`cohort_type = "pos_only"`)

In many clinical studies, only individuals who test positive on baseline screening ($X_{i,1} = 1$) are enrolled into longitudinal follow-up. Because test specificity $\text{spec}_1 < 1$, a fraction of test-positive individuals are false positives ($Z_i = 0, X_{i,1} = 1$) who can never progress to active TB. By Bayes' rule, the effective uncured fraction $\tilde{\pi}_i$ among test-positives is the **Positive Predictive Value**:

$$
\tilde{\pi}_i = \text{PPV}_i = P(Z_i = 1 \mid X_{i,1} = 1) = \frac{\pi_i \, \text{sens}_1}{\pi_i \, \text{sens}_1 + (1 - \pi_i)(1 - \text{spec}_1)},
$$

and the survival mixture cure likelihood for the test-positive cohort becomes:

$$
L_{\text{pos-only}, i}(t_i, d_i) = \left[ \text{PPV}_i \, f_u(t_i) \right]^{d_i} \left[ (1 - \text{PPV}_i) + \text{PPV}_i \, S_u(t_i) \right]^{1 - d_i}.
$$

---

### 4. Parametric Uncured Survival Families (`surv_dist`)

`EvidSynthTB` supports three parametric families for the uncured progression time distribution:

| Distribution (`surv_dist`) | Hazard $h_u(t)$ | Uncured Survival $S_u(t)$ | Parameters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`"gompertz"`** | $h_u(t) = \lambda \exp(\gamma t)$ | $S_u(t) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lambda}{\gamma}\left(e^{\gamma t} - 1\right)\right)$ | Rate $\lambda > 0$, shape $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$ |
| **`"weibull"`** | $h_u(t) = \lambda \gamma t^{\gamma - 1}$ | $S_u(t) = \exp\!\left(-\lambda t^{\gamma}\right)$ | Rate $\lambda > 0$, shape $\gamma > 0$ |
| **`"exponential"`** | $h_u(t) = \lambda$ | $S_u(t) = \exp(-\lambda t)$ | Rate $\lambda > 0$ ($\gamma = 0$) |

---

## Worked Examples

```{r setup-pkg}
library(EvidSynthTB)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

### Example 1: Population vs. Latent-Class Coupling with Dual Tests ($K = 2$)

```{r coupling-example}
sim_k2 <- create_fake_data(
  N_surv = 300,
  n_survey = 1000,
  p_ltbi = 0.30,
  sens = c(0.85, 0.78),
  spec = c(0.95, 0.90),
  surv_dist = "gompertz",
  shape = 0.15,
  rate = 0.10,
  seed = 301
)

fit_pop <- evidsynth_fit(
  prevalence_data = sim_k2$prevalence_data,
  progression_data = sim_k2$progression_data[, c("t", "d", "x1")],
  model = "joint",
  coupling = "population",
  imperfect_test = TRUE,
  chains = 1,
  n_iter = 400,
  n_burnin = 200,
  seed = 301
)

fit_lc_k2 <- evidsynth_fit(
  prevalence_data = sim_k2$prevalence_data,
  progression_data = sim_k2$progression_data[, c("t", "d", "x1", "x2")],
  model = "joint",
  coupling = "latent_class",
  imperfect_test = TRUE,
  chains = 1,
  n_iter = 400,
  n_burnin = 200,
  seed = 301
)

comp_lc <- structure(
  list(
    fits = list(population_1test = fit_pop, latent_class_2tests = fit_lc_k2),
    summary_table = bind_rows(
      mutate(fit_pop$summary, model = "population_1test"),
      mutate(fit_lc_k2$summary, model = "latent_class_2tests")
    )
  ),
  class = "evidsynth_comparison"
)

knitr::kable(
  evaluate_comparison(comp_lc, truth = sim_k2$truth)$parameter_metrics,
  digits = 3
)
```

### Example 2: Test-Positive Follow-Up Cohort (`cohort_type = "pos_only"`)

```{r pos-only-example}
sim_pos <- create_fake_data(
  N_surv = 500,
  n_survey = 1200,
  p_ltbi = 0.30,
  sens = 0.85,
  spec = 0.92,
  surv_dist = "gompertz",
  shape = 0.10,
  rate = 0.12,
  cohort_type = "pos_only",
  seed = 302
)

# True baseline prevalence is 0.30, whereas true PPV among test-positives is ~0.82
c(true_p_ltbi = sim_pos$truth$p_ltbi, true_ppv = round(sim_pos$truth$ppv_surv, 3))

comp_pos <- compare_evidsynth(
  prevalence_data = sim_pos$prevalence_data,
  progression_data = sim_pos$progression_data[, c("t", "d")],
  models = c("joint", "cut"),
  cohort_type = "pos_only",
  imperfect_test = TRUE,
  chains = 1,
  n_iter = 400,
  n_burnin = 200,
  n_cut_subsamples = 10,
  seed = 302
)

knitr::kable(
  evaluate_comparison(comp_pos, truth = sim_pos$truth)$parameter_metrics,
  digits = 3
)
```

### Example 3: Comparing Parametric Survival Families via WAIC

```{r surv-dist-example}
fit_weib <- evidsynth_fit(
  prevalence_data = sim_k2$prevalence_data,
  progression_data = sim_k2$progression_data[, c("t", "d")],
  model = "joint",
  surv_dist = "weibull",
  chains = 1,
  n_iter = 400,
  n_burnin = 200,
  seed = 303
)

fit_exp <- evidsynth_fit(
  prevalence_data = sim_k2$prevalence_data,
  progression_data = sim_k2$progression_data[, c("t", "d")],
  model = "joint",
  surv_dist = "exponential",
  chains = 1,
  n_iter = 400,
  n_burnin = 200,
  seed = 303
)

comp_families <- structure(
  list(
    fits = list(gompertz = fit_pop, weibull = fit_weib, exponential = fit_exp)
  ),
  class = "evidsynth_comparison"
)

knitr::kable(diagnose_feedback(comp_families), digits = 3)
plot_survival_comparison(comp_families, type = "uncured")
```
